text_html: A 43-year-old man comes to the office because of a 5-day history of right-sided back and buttock pain that radiates to the lateral aspect of his right foot. The pain began suddenly after he lifted some bags of cement. The pain is more severe with standing and walking and improves when he lies down. Treatment with ibuprofen has provided only minimal relief. He appears to be in moderate distress. Temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), pulse is 96/min, and blood pressure is 138/88 mm Hg. Physical examination discloses a paraspinal spasm in the lumbar region on the right. A straight-leg raise test result is positive on the right. MRIs of the lumbar and sacral spine (S1) are shown; the arrow indicates an abnormality. Which of the following additional physical examination findings is most likely in this patient?
explanation_html:
Educational Objective: This patient presents with symptoms of acute lumbar radiculopathy and MRI findings of a right-sided disc herniation at L5–S1. The most likely additional physical examination finding is loss of the right ankle reflex.

Evaluation: Lumbar radiculopathy may present with sensory changes, pain, altered deep tendon reflexes, or weakness in the lower extremities, with symptoms corresponding to the affected lumbar root level.

Definition: Lumbar radiculopathy, caused by nerve root compression, may develop due to various causes, including intervertebral disc herniation or lumbar degenerative changes. The L4–L5 and L5–S1 levels are the most commonly involved. Diagnostic testing includes lumbar MRI and nerve conduction studies if needed.

Prevention: Risk factors for lumbar radiculopathy include frequent heavy lifting, sedentary lifestyle, trauma, and obesity.

Treatment: Treatment for lumbar radiculopathy without red flag symptoms (eg, saddle anesthesia, new bowel or bladder deficits) is often conservative with medication management and physical therapy. If symptoms are refractory, epidural corticosteroid injections or operative management may be considered.

Differential: This patient presents with right lower extremity radicular low back pain with a positive straight leg test. Because of the distribution of his symptoms and findings of a right-sided L5–S1 disc herniation on MRI, lumbar radiculopathy is the most likely diagnosis. Loss of the right ankle reflex is the most likely additional physical examination finding as this reflex is mediated by the S1 nerve.

Incorrect Answers: A, B, C, E, F, and G.

Choice A and Choice G: Left quadriceps weakness and right quadriceps weakness are incorrect. The quadriceps muscles are innervated by the femoral nerve, which receives contribution from the L2–L4 nerves. This patient’s radicular pattern and MRI findings are more indicative of a right S1 lumbar radiculopathy.

Choice B: Loss of left ankle reflex is incorrect. This patient is not experiencing left-sided symptoms. Loss of the right ankle reflex is more likely.

Choice C and Choice E: Loss of left patellar reflex and loss of right patellar reflex are incorrect. The patellar reflex is mediated by the L2–L4 nerves. This patient likely has a right S1 lumbar radiculopathy due to the distribution of his radicular symptoms along the lateral foot and MRI findings of a L5–S1 disc herniation.

Choice F: Right hip flexor weakness is incorrect. The hip flexors primarily receive their innervation from the L2–L4 nerve roots. This patient is more likely to have loss of the right ankle reflex due to an underlying right S1 lumbar radiculopathy.
